links.why: Every normal mode is a quantum harmonic oscillator: $E=\hbar\omega(n+\frac12)$. The Einstein solid is $3N$ copies of the QM oscillator; Debye adds a spectrum of $\omega$.
Debye's $T^3$ law is Planck's $T^4$ energy density for a gas of bosons with $\omega=vq$: phonons ($3$ polarisations, speed $v$) versus photons ($2$, speed $c$). See the Degenerate Core room.
Blackbody radiation: the photon version of the phonon gas.

intro: Beneath the caverns the atoms ring like bells. Solve the two-atom chain for its acoustic and optical branches, count phonons with Bose–Einstein statistics and use them to explain why the specific heat of a solid goes as $T^3$ at low temperature and saturates at $3Nk_B$ at high temperature.

blocks.html: Atoms in a crystal are coupled harmonic oscillators. Plane-wave ansatz $u_n\propto e^{i(qna-\omega t)}$ turns Newton's equations into an eigenvalue problem of the dynamical matrix $D(q)$; its eigenvalues are $\omega^2$. With $m$ atoms per cell there are $3m$ branches: 3 acoustic ($\omega\to0$ for $q\to0$), $3(m-1)$ optical.

blocks.label: Nearest-neighbour springs k, mass M, spacing a.
(2.37); gap at q = π/a between √(2k/M_heavy) and √(2k/M_light).

blocks.html: Acoustic: neighbouring atoms move together (sound). Optical: the two atoms of a cell move against each other, so in an ionic crystal the mode has an oscillating dipole and couples to infrared light. At the zone edge $d\omega/dq=0$: standing waves, the phonon is Bragg-reflected by the lattice just like an electron.

Quantisation: each normal mode is a harmonic oscillator, $E=\hbar\omega(n+\frac12)$; the quantum $\hbar\omega$ is a phonon, a boson with $\langle n\rangle=1/(e^{\hbar\omega/k_BT}-1)$. Crystal momentum $\hbar q$ is defined modulo $\hbar G$. Inelastic neutron scattering measures $\omega(q)$ directly.
Branch counting is in 3D: NaCl (2 atoms/cell) has 3 acoustic + 3 optical branches, not 1D's 1+1 (HS20 MC (i)). And $q$ only runs over the first BZ: $q$ and $q+G$ are the same vibration.

blocks.html: Einstein: all modes at one $\omega_E$, $C/3Nk_B=x^2e^x/(e^x-1)^2$ with $x=\Theta_E/T$. Correct at high $T$ (Dulong–Petit), exponentially too small at low $T$; good for flat optical branches.

'Active modes': at temperature $T$ only modes with $\hbar\omega\lesssim k_BT$ are excited, each classically ($k_B$). For acoustic phonons these fill a sphere of radius $q=k_BT/\hbar v$ in $q$-space: number $\propto T^3$. That is the whole $T^3$ law (2.40-2.41); the same counting with photons gives Stefan–Boltzmann.
Fraction of Dulong–Petit at low $T$: $\frac{4\pi^4}{5}(T/T_D)^3=77.9\,(T/T_D)^3$, not $\frac{12\pi^4}5(\ldots)$. And in metals add the electronic $\gamma T$: $C=\gamma T+\beta T^3$.
HS20 MC (l): Einstein assumes a flat dispersion ($\delta$-function DOS), not a linear one. Aug 2024 2b: Debye DOS $\propto1/(V_0\omega_D^3)$, number of phonons at high $T$ $\propto T/\Theta_D$.

check.q: At $T=T_D/10$ the Debye low-temperature formula gives $C_V$ as a fraction of $3Nk_B$ of about
check.explain: $77.9\times10^{-3}=0.078$ (the exact Debye function at $T_D/10$ is a bit lower, 0.07, as the $T^3$ law starts to fail).

check.q: Why does the Einstein model fail at low temperature?
options: its density of states has a gap: no modes below ħω_E
check.explain: Real crystals have gapless acoustic phonons, so some modes are always excitable: power law instead of $e^{-\Theta_E/T}$.

questions.q: How many phonon branches does the dispersion of the NaCl lattice have?
questions.explain: Two atoms per primitive cell, three dimensions.

questions.q: Which statement about the Einstein model is FALSE?
options: it gives good values of c(T) at high T
at high T it agrees with Dulong–Petit
the density of states is a δ-function
it assumes a linear dispersion so all modes have the same velocity
questions.explain: Einstein's modes have one frequency: a flat dispersion with zero group velocity.

questions.q: In an optical mode at $q=0$ of a diatomic chain the centre of mass of each cell
options: moves opposite to the neighbouring cell
questions.explain: $M_1u_1+M_2u_2=0$: the two atoms move against each other.

questions.q: Which material has the highest Debye temperature?
questions.explain: Light and stiff: diamond 2240 K; Pb 105 K, Cu 343 K, Al 428 K (script 2.4.2).

questions.q: For $M_1\to M_2$ the gap at the zone boundary of the diatomic chain
options: closes, and the BZ effectively doubles
questions.explain: Identical atoms: the true period is $a/2$, one branch in a twice larger zone (Fig. 2.2).

questions.q: The low-temperature heat capacity of an insulator goes as
questions.explain: Debye; a metal adds $\gamma T$ from the electrons.

encounters.title: Dispersion of the monatomic chain
encounters.goal: Atoms of mass $M$ at $x_n=na$, nearest-neighbour springs $k$. Derive $\omega(q)$, its long-wavelength limit and the group velocity, and explain why $q$ can be restricted to the first Brillouin zone.

steps.reveal: $q\to q+2\pi/a$ changes $e^{iqna}$ by $e^{2\pi in}=1$: the displacements of the atoms are identical. Only $N$ distinct $q$ exist for $N$ atoms (periodic boundary conditions): one per atom per direction.

keyPoints: $q$ defined modulo $2\pi/a$: N states in the first BZ

encounters.title: A diatomic chain: acoustic and optical branches
encounters.problem: Script 2.2.5: $N$ cells of lattice constant $a$, two atoms per cell (masses $M_1,M_2$ at fractional positions $0$ and $\frac12$), nearest-neighbour springs $k$, longitudinal motion. The dispersion is $\omega^2=k\big(\tfrac1{M_1}+\tfrac1{M_2}\big)\pm k\sqrt{\big(\tfrac1{M_1}+\tfrac1{M_2}\big)^2-\tfrac{2}{M_1M_2}(1-\cos qa)}$. Take a toy NaCl chain: $M_1=22.99\,$u (Na), $M_2=35.45\,$u (Cl), $k=15$ N/m, $a=5.64$ Å. Give frequencies as $\nu=\omega/2\pi$ in THz.

steps.prompt: Optical branch at $q=0$: $\omega=\sqrt{2k(1/M_1+1/M_2)}$. Give $\nu$ in THz.
steps.hint: At $q=0$: $(1-\cos qa)=0$, the root is $2k(1/M_1+1/M_2)$ (plus sign) or 0 (acoustic). The two atoms in the cell move against each other.

steps.prompt: Acoustic branch at the zone edge $q=\pi/a$ (the upper end of the acoustic branch is set by the **heavier** mass): $\nu=\frac1{2\pi}\sqrt{2k/M_2}$ in THz.
steps.hint: At $q=\pi/a$, $1-\cos qa=2$ and the square root becomes $k|1/M_1-1/M_2|$, so $\omega^2=2k/M_{\max}$ (acoustic) and $2k/M_{\min}$ (optical).
Lighter atom oscillates against a nearly still heavy neighbour.

steps.prompt: Frequency gap at the zone boundary in THz (nothing propagates in the gap).
steps.hint: $\Delta\propto 1/\sqrt{M_1}-1/\sqrt{M_2}\to0$ for $M_1\to M_2$: then the zone folds and one branch remains (script, Fig. 2.2). At the boundary both group velocities vanish: $\omega(q)=\omega(-q)$ and $\omega(q+2\pi/a)=\omega(q)$ force $d\omega/dq=0$ at $q=\pi/a$.

steps.prompt: Sound velocity from the small-$q$ acoustic branch $\omega\approx vq$ with $v=a\sqrt{k/[2(M_1+M_2)]}$, in m/s.
steps.hint: Expand $\omega^2\approx\frac{k\,a^2}{2(M_1+M_2)}q^2$. Check: for $M_1=M_2=M$ this is $(a/2)\sqrt{k/M}$, the monatomic chain with spacing $a/2$.

steps.prompt: Energy $\hbar\omega$ of the optical $q=0$ phonon in meV (this is what inelastic neutron scattering measures).
steps.hint: $\hbar\omega=h\nu$; 1 THz = 4.136 meV. Thermal neutrons ($\sim25$ meV) match phonon energies.

encounters.title: Copper: where do phonons stop mattering?
encounters.problem: Copper has $n=8.47\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$ atoms, one conduction electron each, and Debye temperature $T_D=343$ K (script 2.4). Free-electron gas: $c_{\rm el}=\frac{\pi^2}{3}\nu(\epsilon_F)k_B^2T=\gamma T$ with $\nu(\epsilon_F)=\frac{3n}{2\epsilon_F}$. Debye low-$T$ law (script 2.79): $c_{\rm ph}=\frac{12\pi^4}{5}\,nk_B\,(T/T_D)^3=\beta T^3$. Find the temperature where both contribute equally.

steps.prompt: Dulong–Petit limit $3nk_B$ of the lattice heat capacity per volume, in J m$^{-3}$ K$^{-1}$.
steps.hint: Classical equipartition: $3k_B$ per atom, valid for $T\gtrsim T_D$ (script 2.80).
$k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}=1.36$ Å$^{-1}$, $\hbar^2/2m_e=3.81$ eV Å$^2$. One electron per atom.

steps.prompt: Electronic coefficient $\gamma=\frac{\pi^2}{2}\,\frac{nk_B^2}{\epsilon_F}$ in J m$^{-3}$ K$^{-2}$.
steps.hint: $\frac{\pi^2}{3}\nu k_B^2=\frac{\pi^2}{3}\frac{3n}{2\epsilon_F}k_B^2$. Only electrons within $k_BT$ of $\epsilon_F$ (a fraction $T/T_F$) can absorb heat.

steps.prompt: Phonon coefficient $\beta=\frac{12\pi^4}{5}nk_B/T_D^3$ in J m$^{-3}$ K$^{-4}$.
steps.hint: $12\pi^4/5=233.8$. Debye assumes $\nu(\epsilon)\propto\epsilon^2$ up to a cutoff that holds $3N$ modes.

steps.prompt: Crossover temperature $\gamma T=\beta T^3$, i.e. $T_\times=\sqrt{\gamma/\beta}$, in K.
steps.hint: Below $T_\times$ electrons dominate $C_V\propto T$; above it phonons $\propto T^3$. Plotting $C/T$ against $T^2$ gives a straight line with intercept $\gamma$ and slope $\beta$. Here $T_\times\approx3$ K, well inside the $T^3$ regime ($T<T_D/50\approx7$ K).

encounters.title: Einstein versus Debye at low temperature
encounters.problem: A solid has a single Einstein temperature $\Theta_E=300$ K (all $3N$ modes at one frequency, $\nu(\epsilon)\propto\delta(\hbar\omega_E-\epsilon)$) and, in the Debye model, $T_D=300$ K. Heat capacity as a fraction of $3Nk_B$: Einstein $f_E(x)=x^2e^x/(e^x-1)^2$ with $x=\Theta_E/T$; Debye low-$T$: $f_D=\frac{4\pi^4}{5}(T/T_D)^3$ (this is $C_V/3Nk_B$; the script's (2.79) $C_V=\frac{12\pi^4}{5}Nk_B(T/T_D)^3$ divided by the Dulong–Petit value $3Nk_B$).

steps.hint: Ratio of the oscillator quantum to $k_BT$.
At $x=3$ about half of the classical Dulong–Petit value: the oscillators are partly frozen out.

$\frac{4\pi^4}{5}=77.9$, so $77.9\times(0.05)^3=0.0097$: about 1 % of the classical value (and the exact Debye function agrees). The $T^3$ law needs only the **linear** acoustic dispersion at small $q$.
For $x\gg1$: $f_E\to x^2e^{-x}$, an activated (exponential) freeze-out: far too fast. Einstein's model has a gap at $\epsilon=\hbar\omega_E$, real solids have gapless acoustic phonons.

steps.prompt: How many times larger is the Debye value than the Einstein value at $T_2$? (quick estimate within 25 %)
steps.hint: That is why Einstein's 1907 model failed experiment at low $T$ and Debye's gives the $T^3$ law. Einstein remains the right tool for flat optical branches (script 2.4.2).

encounters.title: Why neutrons and not X-rays?
encounters.problem: Quick fight. Phonon energies are of order 10 meV, and inelastic scattering needs the probe energy to be comparable. Take a thermal neutron with the exam's $\lambda=2.36$ Å ($\hbar^2k^2/2m_n$) and compare it with an X-ray photon of the same wavelength ($E=hc/\lambda$). Ratio in a factor of 1.3.

steps.hint: A $10$ meV phonon changes a 5 keV photon's energy by one part in $5\times10^5$: practically unresolvable. For neutrons the same energy transfer is a $\sim70\%$ effect. Same wavelength (atomic spacing), very different energy: the neutron is the phonon probe. Bridge to QM: de Broglie $\lambda=h/p$.

encounters.instructions: No written phonon problem exists in the recent exams, so this one is built from the script derivation and the oral-exam checklist. Do it on paper, then check the numbers.
statement: A one-dimensional crystal has two atoms per unit cell of length $a$, with masses $M_1=M$ and $M_2=3M$, coupled only to nearest neighbours by springs of constant $k$.
(a) [5 pt] Write the equations of motion for the displacements $\rho_{i,1},\rho_{i,2}$ and derive the dispersion $\omega^2(q)$ with the plane-wave ansatz.
(b) [3 pt] Sketch both branches over $-2\pi/a<q<2\pi/a$. Mark the first Brillouin zone and the group velocity at $q=\pi/a$. Why does it vanish?
(c) [4 pt] Give $\omega$ of the acoustic and optical branches at $q=0$ and $q=\pi/a$ in units of $\sqrt{k/M}$. For $q\to0$ describe the atomic motion in both branches.
(d) [3 pt] What happens to the gap at $q=\pi/a$ for $M_2\to M_1$? Explain through the folding of the Brillouin zone.
(e) [3 pt] The crystal is probed by inelastic neutron scattering with $\lambda=2.36$ Å. Why can this energy window resolve $\hbar\omega(q)$?
keyPoints: (a) $M_1\ddot\rho_{i,1}=-k(2\rho_{i,1}-\rho_{i,2}-\rho_{i-1,2})$ and $M_2\ddot\rho_{i,2}=-k(2\rho_{i,2}-\rho_{i,1}-\rho_{i+1,1})$; ansatz $\rho_{i,\alpha}=A_\alpha e^{i(qia-\omega t)}/\sqrt{M_\alpha}$ gives the $2\times2$ dynamical matrix $D$ with $D_{11}=2k/M_1$, $D_{22}=2k/M_2$, $D_{12}=-k(1+e^{iqa})/\sqrt{M_1M_2}$, and $\det(D-\omega^2)=0$.

(b) The acoustic branch starts at 0, the optical at $\omega_{\rm opt}(0)$. Both flatten at $q=\pi/a$ because $\omega(q)=\omega(-q)$ and $\omega(q)=\omega(q+2\pi/a)$, so $d\omega/dq=0$ at the zone edge (standing waves, Bragg reflection of the phonon).

(c) $q=0$: acoustic 0, optical $\sqrt{2(1+1/3)}\sqrt{k/M}=1.63\sqrt{k/M}$; $q=\pi/a$: acoustic $\sqrt{2k/M_2}=0.82\sqrt{k/M}$, optical $\sqrt{2k/M_1}=1.41\sqrt{k/M}$. Acoustic at $q\to0$: both atoms in phase (sound wave); optical: the two atoms of a cell move against each other, centre of mass at rest.

(d) The gap $\propto|1/\sqrt{M_1}-1/\sqrt{M_2}|$ closes: the cell has halved to $a/2$ with one atom per cell, the Brillouin zone doubles, and the two branches are one branch in the extended zone (Fig. 2.2). Same story for a dimerisation: the gap opens as the cell doubles.

(e) $\lambda=2.36$ Å gives $E_n\approx15$ meV, matching $\hbar\omega$ of phonons (10–100 meV) while its momentum $2\pi/\lambda\approx2.7$ Å$^{-1}$ is large compared with $\pi/a$: the transfers of both energy and momentum can be read off. X-rays of the same $\lambda$ have keV energy: the phonon energy is far below the resolution.
